name: Nishiki-e multi-block colour woodblock print
summary: A drawing is pasted on a cherry plank and cut by a carver. A printer rubs water-based pigment from one block for each colour onto damp washi with a baren. The colours are flat and soft, and the wood grain shows.

philosophy.core_thesis: A set of wood blocks, one for each colour, can make a full-colour picture when a printer rubs thin water-based colour into damp paper and keeps each block in register by hand.
design_principles: Print a sumi key block first. Keep its line 0.2–0.5 mm wide and unbroken, so the carver can follow it.
Give each flat colour its own block. Use 3–12 blocks, and let the inks mix where two colours overlap.
Cut two L-shaped register marks (kento) on each block, so each colour lands on the key line within 0.5 mm.
Make a gradation (bokashi) by wiping the ink on the block with a damp cloth. Place it at the sky, the water and the hem of a robe.
Leave the wood grain in the large flat areas. Do not hide it with extra ink.
Press a bare, inkless block into the sheet (karazuri) where you need a raised line, for example on snow or a collar.
Print on thin damp washi, and rub the back with a baren in a circle until the colour sinks into the fibre.
anti_patterns: A thick, even outline round each shape
A smooth digital gradient with no hand-wipe edge
A halftone dot or a photographic tone
Perfect register with no kento shift or grain

process.matrix: Planks of mountain cherry (yamazakura), cut on both faces, with one block for each colour and a key block with kento register notches.
process.press: No press. A printer rubs the back of the sheet with a baren, a disc of bamboo-sheath cord, by hand.
process.image_making: A publisher commissions the work. The artist draws in ink, a carver cuts the key block, and a printer sets and prints the colour blocks.
process.edition: A few hundred to several thousand sheets for each design, and the blocks can be recut for reprints.

inks.strategy: Water-based pigment and rice paste. The key block prints first in sumi, then each colour block prints in turn from light to dark.

screening.rule: Make a tone with a flat colour field or with a wiped bokashi gradation of 10–40 mm. The style has no hatching and no dot.

registration.rule: The kento marks hold each colour within 0.5 mm of the key line, and a small gap or overlap of colour at an edge is normal.

substrate.stock: Hand-made washi of mulberry fibre (kozo), thin and damp when printed.
substrate.finish: Unsized or lightly sized, with a soft surface and visible long fibres.

surface.impression: Light. The baren leaves a faint circular sheen on the back, and an embossed (karazuri) line stands up in fine work.
surface.sheen: Matt, with a soft shine on burnished or mica areas.
surface.texture: Flat colour with the wood grain in it, soft wiped edges, and the long fibres of the paper.

emotion.target_response: Calm, flat beauty: the viewer reads a soft, clear picture that many hands made, with a fine eye for season and weather.

avoid_when: The picture needs a photographic tone or a sharp, glossy finish.
The brief needs a heavy, bold outline or a pop colour set.

modifiers.how: Keep the block and the washi. Let one artist cut the block, show the gouge marks, and use fewer, bolder colours.
Keep the process. Add 8–12 tonal blocks and wiped gradations for rain, dusk and lamp light.
Reduce the sheet to a small square. Add embossing, metallic dust and a verse beside the image.
